report:
The claim that "acupuncture reduces depression symptoms during pregnancy" is not clearly false — it's better characterized as preliminary/uncertain rather than debunked.

The main evidence is a single RCT by Manber et al. (2010), which randomized 150 pregnant women with major depressive disorder to depression-specific acupuncture, control (non-specific) acupuncture, or massage. The depression-specific group showed significantly greater symptom reduction and a response rate about 20% higher than controls (https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/10.1097/aog.0b013e3181cc0816~acupuncture-for-depression-during-pregnancy-a-randomized). Stanford's press coverage of the same trial states acupuncture "appears to be an effective way to reduce depression symptoms during pregnancy" (https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2010/02/acupuncture-lessens-depression-symptoms-during-pregnancy-study-shows.html). However, the lead investigator Rachel Manber is quoted cautioning: "I don't think we have a universal conclusion at this point that acupuncture works for depression, but we do have some evidence that's growing" (https://health.usnews.com/health-news/blogs/on-women/2010/02/22/acupuncture-may-help-alleviate-depression-during-pregnancy).

A follow-up review notes: "Preliminary evidence is suggestive that acupuncture may provide a safe and effective alternative treatment option for antenatal depression; however, additional research is required," calling for further trials (Ormsby/Dahlen protocol paper cited via https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13063-016-1204-9). A broader meta-analysis (PLOS ONE) also found "positive results" for acupuncture as an adjunct treatment, alongside CBT and body-oriented interventions (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0173397).

**Conclusion:** The claim is not false, but the evidence is limited—based mainly on one moderately-sized trial plus supportive but tentative reviews calling for more research. It's more accurate to say evidence is promising but not yet definitive, rather than the claim being false.
